title: Hantavirus outbreak forces cruise passengers to leave ship at St Helena - News On AIR

analysis.time: The outbreak was reported to have occurred last month, with the first passenger death on April 11, and the ship anchored near Cape Verde for three days. The three patients were transferred from the ship in late May, and two were evacuated to the Netherlands for treatment.
analysis.location_and_population: The cruise ship MV Hondius, carrying passengers and crew from 23 different countries, was anchored near Cape Verde. The ship was en route to Spain’s Canary Islands, and passengers disembarked at St Helena, an island in the South Atlantic.
analysis.event: A hantavirus outbreak on the cruise ship MV Hondius led to the disembarkation of around 40 passengers at St Helena, with three deaths reported among those who were aboard the ship since it set sail from Argentina a month ago. The Dutch Foreign Ministry confirmed the number of affected individuals.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Three passengers died, and two were in serious condition and evacuated to the Netherlands. A third passenger remained aboard a delayed evacuation flight. The outbreak involves the Andes strain of hantavirus, which has limited human-to-human transmission. Authorities in Europe, South Africa, and Argentina are conducting contact tracing, quarantine planning, and laboratory testing.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The ship operator, Oceanwide Expeditions, stated that the body of the Dutch man who died was taken off at St Helena, and his wife also disembarked there. The company had not previously acknowledged that dozens more people left the ship at that time. The World Health Organisation identified the outbreak as likely involving the Andes strain.

The outbreak is linked to the Andes strain of hantavirus, which has limited human-to-human transmission. The ship, carrying passengers and crew from 23 countries, is now sailing towards Spain’s Canary Islands under strict precautionary measures. Authorities in Europe, South Africa, and Argentina are conducting contact tracing, quarantine planning, and laboratory testing to contain the outbreak. The ship operator, Oceanwide Expeditions, had not previously acknowledged that dozens more people left the ship at St Helena, where the body of a Dutch man who died was taken off. The World Health Organisation identified the outbreak as likely involving the Andes strain, which can transmit between close contacts. The three suspected hantavirus patients, of British, Dutch, and German nationalities, were transferred by medical evacuation teams in full hazmat gear.

analysis.location_and_population: Cruise ship MV Hondius; passengers and crew aboard the vessel; global population assessed for risk.

analysis.brief_en: A rare Andes virus outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius earlier in 2026 resulted in three deaths and 13 infections among passengers and crew, according to a commentary published in JAMA Internal Medicine by researchers from the University of Maryland School of Medicine. While the event drew parallels to early COVID-19 dynamics due to its cruise-ship setting, experts clarified that Andes virus has limited human-to-human transmission, making a larger outbreak improbable. The authors underscored the need for evidence-based communication to prevent public fear from overshadowing scientific realities, noting that Andes virus outbreaks historically remain small and self-limited. The commentary also highlighted the importance of robust international public health networks and sustained investment in vaccines and therapeutics for emerging infectious diseases.
